Long-Bodied Grey Dog: Filler that mostly doesn't make the cut. Flash and reach look like they should matter, but there is almost no flying in the set and the Treasure buys nothing worth splashing for. A 22.8% play rate against a 52.3% GIH is the shape of a card only played when a deck is short.
Old Thrush: A cut in almost every deck. Two mana for a 1/2 flier and 2 life is below rate, and tutoring a basic to the *top* costs you your next draw — bad fixing in a format where you shouldn't be splashing anyway. The 23.4% play rate is the verdict.
Troop of Ponies: Overrated by LR's B. Two mana for a 2/1 that sacrifices to fetch two basics is fixing for a format that doesn't want to splash, and the 53.3% GIH bears that out. Play it only if you are genuinely three colours, which you shouldn't be.
Belladonna Took: Underwhelming for a rare and the numbers agree — a 52.2% GIH with a negative IWD despite a 70.4% play rate means people are picking it and being disappointed. It needs three token triggers in one turn to do anything memorable, and only a dedicated W/U recruit board gets there.
Bilbo's Gambit: A fringe playable with no measured win rate at 33.6% play — most white decks correctly leave it out. Gifting a Treasure to accelerate the opponent is a real cost in a format this fast, and the effect isn't worth the two mana plus the gift. Provisional read.
Bofur, Reliable Guardian: A useful R/W and W/U uncommon that never rots in your hand. A one-mana lifelink legend is fine storied fodder, and holding the adventure as a two-mana protection spell blanks a removal spell or wins a combat. Two cards in one slot at a modest rate.
Celebrate the Mountain-king: The premier splash card in the set and every source agrees. Four mana to exile any nonland permanent and recruit is removal plus a body plus card selection on one card, and the single white pip makes it castable from almost any deck. A 62.6% GIH at 88.9% play is elite for an uncommon.
Dáin, Lord of the Iron Hills: A fine R/W two-drop rather than the B− LR gave it. Vigilance on a 2/2 is real, and the Propaganda clause with an enduring story genuinely taxes a go-wide opponent. The +1.5 IWD says it's a solid playable that occasionally locks up a race.
Dwarven Provisioner: Solid R/W and W/U playable and the best of white's three common team-pumps. The body is unexciting but the four-mana anthem activation is a real mana sink in a format with almost no sweepers, where going wide is rewarded. The −0.5 IWD understates it; this is a board-presence card, not a swing card.
Dwarven Shortsword: A solid R/W common that plays better than the −1.7 IWD suggests. Four mana for effectively a 3/4 body that leaves a +1/+2 sword behind is two pieces of cardboard, and it counts as an artifact for storied. LLU had it as white's top common; that is roughly right in a colour this thin.
Eagle of the Great Shelf: Mediocre despite being a flier in a set with almost none. Five mana for a 2/5 that only threatens damage in a wide board is too slow, and the 52.7% play rate says half of white decks pass on it. Ben's #2 white uncommon is too high; it's a playable, not a payoff.
The Eagles Are Coming!: A top-three rare and a genuine first pick. Two mana to save a creature from removal and get a 4/4 flier is already fine; kicked for six it picks up your whole board and returns it as a squadron of fliers. Remember the birds arrive at the *next* upkeep, so cast it on your turn if you want to attack.
Esgaroth Garrison: Only playable in a go-wide W/U board and rarely even then. Five mana for a */5 that recruits is fine value, but the 19.6% play rate and ALSA 7.5 say it wheels every time. Take a two-drop instead.
Fíli the Pathfinder: The best card in the set — a +13.9 IWD at ALSA 1.9 is the highest combination here. Four mana for two 2/2 bodies is already fine, and the team-wide +1/+1 with an enduring story turns every subsequent dwarf into a threat. Storied switches on almost immediately in R/W. First pick, every time.
Gleaming Splendor: Unplayable despite the mythic slot — 24.9% play and no measured win rate. Making Treasures off the opponent's draws is a Constructed engine, and two mana that affects nothing on board is a losing turn. Provisional read, but the F grade looks right.
Iron Hills Blacksmith: Excellent in R/W and better than its rate suggests — 59.0% GIH at 86.8% play. Double strike means every equipment you attach counts twice, the Axe token is a free artifact for storied, and it's two permanents from one card. Ethan's #2 white uncommon is right.
Kíli the Resourceful: First-pickable and a must-kill on turn two. A +11.1 IWD on a two-drop is enormous — it snowballs because free equips and the draw trigger feed each other, and storied switches on almost by accident with 74 enablers in the set. Both LLU reviewers had it top-10 and the data agrees.
Lake-town Lookout: Filler, playable only in W/U where the recruit trigger has payoffs. A one-drop that replaces itself on death is not nothing in a go-wide deck, but it does not affect the board and the 30.1% play rate reflects that. Last card in the deck.
Lake-town Toymaker: Narrow but real in W/U, and much better than its D− grade. A 3/4 body blocks the format well on its own, and the +3/+0 first-strike trigger is a genuine combat blowout in a deck that reliably draws two. The 42.6% play rate is the cost of that conditional.
Magnificent End: White's only common removal and therefore always playable, but the rate is poor. Five damage misses the 6-toughness creatures that matter and it costs four unless the target is tapped, which means it's a reactive card in a proactive format. Take it because white has nothing else.
Moment of Glory: A cut in most decks, and the flashback is the whole point. Its real job is being the card you happily discard to a recruit trigger, after which five mana pumps your whole board. A 50.2% GIH says the maindeck version is replacement-level.
The Mountain-king's Return: Far better than its D+ grade — a 61.5% GIH and +6.4 IWD at 84.3% play. Recruit, then reanimate a three-drop, then a counter is three cards' worth of value for three mana. The risk both guides flagged, needing a creature in the yard, resolves more often than they expected.
Ori, Keeper of Songs: Filler you play to *be* a storied enabler rather than for the body. A three-mana 3/3 is on rate and the vigilance upgrade is minor; the −0.8 IWD says it contributes nothing beyond its stats. Fine in R/W, cut elsewhere.
The Queen of Dale: A strong W/U mythic that rewards a patient deck. Recruiting off their first noncreature spell each turn accumulates real advantage across a long game, and the +6.5 IWD at ALSA 2.0 says it's doing work. Weak against creature-dense aggro decks that cast nothing else.
Roads Go Ever, Ever On: Playable but unexciting, and a trap if you read it as card advantage. Fixing two Plains and gaining 2 does nothing to a board, and in a fast format the Saga's payoff arrives turns after you needed it. The 56.0% is closer to replacement-level than the rare slot suggests.
Settle the Wreckage: Better than LLU's dismissal but not the blowout its reputation implies. A 59.5% GIH and +4.5 IWD say it wins games; the 84.1% play rate says people jam it regardless. It punishes the format's go-wide attacks hard, but against one big creature it is four mana to ramp your opponent. Hold it, and expect good players to play around it.
Stone by Sunlight: The best efficient removal in the set at uncommon and a high pick. Two mana at instant speed to kill anything with power four or greater answers exactly the creatures that matter here, and the indestructible mode blanks a removal spell or wins a fight. An 88.7% play rate at 60.0% is a premium card.
Thorin's Last Stand: Effectively a sideboard card and the 15.8% play rate says most players agree. A 49.1% GIH is below replacement; four mana for a team pump is too slow in a format decided earlier than that. The disenchant mode is the real reason to keep one nearby, given how much equipment is running around.
An Unexpected Party: The best card in the set by IWD — +13.1 is enormous, and a 91.0% play rate at ALSA 1.8 means it's first-picked and always played. At the Door makes an army of dwarves, then the enchantment gives them +2/+2 permanently. Cast the adventure first; the enchantment is the finisher.
Velvetwing Butterflies: The LoL split resolves toward Ben. A 53.2% GIH and 40.0% play rate say Ethan's Ardenvale comparison doesn't hold — it's a 2/2 rather than a 2/3, and the set has no adventure payoffs to reward the split card. Playable filler, not a top white common.
Vow to Erebor: A cut. A 50.5% GIH with a −2.3 IWD at 19.9% play is close to the bottom of the format. Untap plus +2/+2 is a trick with no payoff behind it, and the equipment rider needs a dwarf and an equipment you'd rather have attached already.
Bilbo, Luckwearer: One of blue's best cards and a +9.1 IWD backs both hosts' #1 ranking. A two-mana unblockable looter draws you a card every turn unanswered, and Burglar's Plot means the card is never dead — trade a recruit token for their bomb. Take it early.
Bilbo, Thief in the Night: A build-around whose 57.4% is soft for a mythic, but the +8.1 IWD says it does real work when it connects. Recasting instants and sorceries from the yard rewards a deck with cheap interaction; without that it's a 2/2 that needs to attack. Provisional read on a card most players are still learning.
Bilbo Baggins, Burglar: The best common in the set and every source agrees. Three mana for a 2/1 that draws a card is already fine; the {U} Scry 2 adventure means it is never a dead card and keeps one-land hands live. A +5.9 IWD at common is exceptional.
Confusticate and Bebother: Playable filler in a controlling blue deck. A Force Spike-for-four is unreliable and draw-two-discard-one is a fair rate, so the flexibility is the whole appeal. The 46.2% play rate says most blue decks would rather have a body.
Elrond, Moon-Reader: A build-around mythic with no measured win rate at 64.8% play, which means people try it and it rarely decides games. Drawing a card per activated ability wants an equipment deck it isn't in, and the seven-mana blink is win-more. Provisional read.
Elven Raft-Steerer: A cut. A 48.9% GIH is below replacement, and landfall tap-or-untap doesn't do enough in a blue deck that isn't assertive. LR's C− was right and the 38.8% play rate agrees.
Elvenking's Harper: A cut at 25.8% play. A two-mana 2/2 with a five-mana unblockable activation is a card from a slower format; here the activation never gets paid. LR's D is right.
Enchanted River's Grasp: Blue's cleanest removal and better than Ben's dismissal — a +4.0 IWD at 77.6% play. Stripping counters as it lands is elegantly aimed at amass, and removing abilities answers the format's utility creatures. The bounce and sacrifice Ben worried about doesn't come up as often as he expected.
Fateful Discovery: The least-played card in the set at 0.5% and no measured win rate. Drawing off artifacts entering is a Constructed engine with no support here. Do not play it. Provisional only because essentially nobody has.
Gandalf, Wandering Wizard: A trap, and every source agrees. Five mana for a 4/5 with no immediate impact is exactly the wrong rate in a format decided on the ground, and the six-mana bail-out never gets activated. A 19.5% play rate against a 52.6% GIH is the signature of a card people try once.
Great Gilded Boat: A first-pick rare and splashable from anywhere. A 4/4 that crews for 2 and recruits on every attack converts a board into card advantage, and the +8.7 IWD is among the highest in the set. Take it out of any pack; it does not need a W/U deck to be great.
Lakeshore Apothecary: Ben's hot take is validated — a D grade against a 57.6% GIH and +5.3 IWD is a big gap in the card's favour. Vigilance means it attacks and blocks while growing, and W/U reliably draws a second card. It is a genuine build-around payoff, not filler.
Lake-town Mariners: Too expensive to matter in this format. Six mana for a 6/5 arrives after the game is decided, and Gone Fishing at four is a value blink with nothing worth blinking. A 51.1% GIH and 40.9% play rate say it's the last card in a blue deck.
Long Lake Nuisance: Better than its D+ grade suggests — a +6.6 IWD is one of the highest among blue commons. A 3/1 flier is a real clock in a set with almost no fliers, and the recruit trigger is pure value. The one risk is dying to the format's one-damage sweepers.
The Lord of the Eagles: A build-around finisher that rarely gets built. Nine mana base cost means you need real flying power on board to discount it, and blue is the format's thinnest flier colour. The 53.6% GIH at 58.3% play says it's often a dead card in hand.
Master's Councillors: Considerably better than its D grade. A 1/3 vigilance blocks the format's cheap attackers all day, and it grows to a real threat once graveyards fill. A +5.2 IWD says it's doing more than its stat line, and W/U reliably triggers the second-draw clause.
Mirkwood Meditator: The worst common in the set by play rate — 6.0% at ALSA 8.4, meaning it wheels every single time. A 2/4 that can become a 4/2 is lost between archetypes: too passive for B/G, too slow for G/U. LR's D is right.
Most Decrepit Old Bird: A fine two-for-one that overperforms its rate. Milling four to find an instant or sorcery smooths a blue deck, and the one-mana flier is a real body once threshold turns on. Take it as a playable, not as a reason to be blue.
Old Fat Spider Can't See Me: Slow value that underperforms both guides' B grades. Chapter two neutralising their best threat is real, but a 52.9% GIH says four mana that affects nothing the turn it lands is a poor rate in a fast format. Playable in a controlling blue deck, not a high pick.
Plunder the Trollshaws: A top blue common and a two-for-one across two turns. The instant speed matters more than it reads: flashing it back on their turn triggers draw-two payoffs that a sorcery couldn't, since your draw step already spent the first draw. Perfect card to pitch to recruit.
Ravenhill Flock: A trap and LR called it correctly. A 1/2 flier for four that only grows on draws is exactly the card that reads better than it plays, and a 52.2% GIH confirms it. The +3.7 IWD is the tell that it only looks good in the decks already drawing a lot.
Riddles in the Dark: Underwhelming for a rare at 50.4% GIH. Fact or Fiction is a fine card in the abstract, but three mana that doesn't affect the board is a losing turn here, and the opponent choosing the split blunts it. Playable in a controlling blue deck only.
Roll-Roll-Roll-Roll: The worst card in the set by a wide margin — a 40.3% GIH and −7.6 IWD are both outliers, nearly nine points below the next-worst card. Blinking your own permanent four times does nothing to a board in a format decided by combat. Never play it.
Sound the Trumpets: A weak maindeck card but genuinely better in Sealed, exactly as LR said. Three mana for a hard counter is a fair rate in a slower game; in draft the 39.3% play rate says most decks want a body instead. Keep one in the sideboard.
Thranduil's Decree: Ethan's instinct was better than his initial grade — a 37.4% play rate says most blue decks correctly pass. Six mana for a counter is unaffordable in a format this fast, though the free-cast clause on a permanent is a real blowout when you get there. Sideboard card.
Uncover the Moon-Letters: Unplayable, and the only rare in the set with an F grade and no measured win rate at 7.5% play. It asks a creature-combat format to be a spells deck, and discarding two makes even the successful casts a wash. Provisional only because almost nobody has tried it.
Uneasy Partings: A fine blue common and blue's most reliable answer. Tuck effects don't permanently solve a threat, but the discount against attackers makes it a real tempo play and the +3.0 IWD is honest. Blue is thin on interaction, so take it higher than the C+ grade suggests.
Wizard's Staff: Unplayable — a 15.1% play rate and no measured win rate on a rare. Prowess on an equipped creature does nothing in a creature-combat format with few noncreature spells, and the trigger-doubling clause needs a board you won't have. Provisional read for lack of games.
Along the Crooked Way: The −4.4 IWD is one of the worst in the set and it exposes the card. Three mana that returns a creature and then does nothing on board is a losing turn here, and the menace activation is win-more. A 71.5% play rate means people are over-drafting it on rarity.
Azog, Moria's Ruin: Overdrafted on rarity — ALSA 2.3 and 84.5% play against a −2.3 IWD. The removal is real but it hands your opponent an Army equal to the creature's power, which in a set built around amass is a genuine drawback. Kill something small or don't cast it.
Bilbo's Deadly Slice: Unconditional removal at common and a 93.0% play rate says every black deck plays it. Ben's "Murder's washed" is too harsh — in a format where the only efficient removal is at uncommon, three mana to kill anything is a real card. The double black is the only friction.
Crude Bent Blade: The LR split resolves emphatically toward playable — a 61.1% GIH and +3.1 IWD at 84.5% play is one of the best black commons. An edict that leaves a +2/+1 equipment behind is two cards, and sorcery timing means you choose the moment after their tokens have traded off. Both LoL hosts preferring it to Bilbo's Deadly Slice looks right.
Desolation Prowler: One of the best two-drops in the set and LR's highest-graded card in the review. The threat of activation alone brick-walls 3/3s, and it turns on ferocious by itself. Note it's once each *turn*, so you can pump on both your turn and theirs. A 90.6% play rate at 62.5% is elite.
Down, Down to Goblin-town: Premium B/R uncommon and a first-pick from the pack. Hand disruption, a body, and two drains from one three-mana card is a lot of value in a format where two-for-ones decide games. Both LoL hosts had it #2 in black and LLU said afterwards they had it too low.
Dreaded Bat-Cloud: A good B/R playable that arrives cheap in the deck that wants it. Flying deathtouch on a 4/2 dominates combat, and in a sacrifice deck the cost reduction is close to automatic. LR split on it; the 78.3% play rate says the goblin decks resolved the argument.
Front Porch Sentries: Reasonable B/R filler that trades up. Two mana for a 2/2 is on rate, and the death trigger picks off a 1/1 token, which matters against W/U recruit boards. The −1.5 IWD says it is a body first and a value card second.
Gathering of Darkness: Solid B/R value that the −2.8 IWD undersells. Four mana for a raised creature plus three counters on your Army is two cards' worth of material, and if you already have an Army those counters attack immediately. Good, just not a card that swings a game you were losing.
Gnashing of Teeth: Premium black removal and LoL's #1 black uncommon. −5/−5 with exile answers almost anything, and the −1/−1 sweep mode wrecks recruit tokens and small amass armies. A 91.6% play rate at ALSA 2.8 is what a format staple looks like; sorcery speed is the only knock.
Gollum, Riddle Master: A premium mythic and one of the format's best two-drops. A 3/1 for two already pressures, and the odd/even trigger accumulates counters and drains across a normal game. A 64.1% GIH with a 93.4% play rate at ALSA 1.6 makes it near-unpassable.
Gollum, Silent Slinker: Better than its D+ grade and both guides' splits. A four-mana 4/3 menace is a real threat, and Meager Meal slots into any spare mana for a counter and 2 life. Worth knowing the adventure targets a creature *and* a player, so killing the creature in response doesn't fizzle it.
Gollum the Abandoned: Good in aggressive B/R and mediocre elsewhere — LR's split read is the accurate one. The drain fires even with nothing to exile, so it's two damage on turn two, and the recursion gives a sacrifice deck a mana sink. Can't block, which is a real cost against the format's aggro decks.
Great Fierce Bee: Filler. A three-mana 2/2 flier is a real body in a set this light on evasion, but the scry rider is close to nothing and the 25.5% play rate says most decks find something better. Fine as a 23rd card in a deck short on fliers.
Great Ugly-Looking Goblin: Effectively a two-drop that draws you a six-mana 4/4 — cast Clap! Snap! early for amass 2, then the creature later. The menace rider matters because your Army always has counters on it. A near-90% play rate on an uncommon this expensive says the split cost carries it.
Head of the Hunt: A premium rare and an early pick at ALSA 1.7. Flash makes it an ambush 4/3, and the replacement effect exiles instead of killing while handing you a 2/2 every time — it beats recursion and turns every trade into a two-for-one. A 92.6% play rate on a double-black card says it's worth building toward.
Inside Information: A trap despite the mythic slot, and an F grade the data backs — 50.5% GIH with a −5.9 IWD at 78.2% play. Exiling their top X and paying life to cast it is a slow, expensive way to generate cards in a format that ends on the ground. Take a creature.
The Master of Lake-town: Solid but not a bomb. Deathtouch on a three-mana 3/2 trades up reliably, which is what you want, but the mill clauses are close to irrelevant and the death trigger rarely fires. A 55.4% GIH is a fair playable.
Nighthowl Pursuer: A genuinely good B/G one-drop. Menace means it keeps attacking profitably, and with ferocious online it swings as a 3/3 that two creatures must block. The +0.6 IWD is modest because it needs the enabler, but 59.1% on a one-mana card is strong.
Rage into the Valley: Solid B/R common that the −2.1 IWD undersells. A card, a life, and two counters on your Army for three mana is real material, and if you already have an Army those counters attack immediately. Worse in multiples, since you'd rather have separate bodies.
Ravening Warg: A solid B/G two-drop. Deathtouch trades up against anything, which matters when the format's best creatures are large, and the lifegain rider helps in the races B/G ends up in. A 58.0% GIH on a common is respectable.
Reverent Howl: A cut. Both halves are below rate — draw two lose two does not affect the board when you cast it, and a +2/+2 lifelink trick is not what a two-mana instant should be. The −2.2 IWD is the honest number here; flexibility is not a substitute for impact.
Rhovanion Rampager: An early first pick and the LLU disagreement is settled: Mark's A− was closer than Alex's C−. ALSA 1.8 and a 93.1% play rate mean it is taken and played almost every time, and the floor — a 3/2 that dies into a 3/3 Army — is why. Premium in B/R and B/G alike.
The Sackville-Bagginses: Strong in B/R and better than its C− grade. Sacrificing a token or spare artifact to draw a card and make a Treasure is pure value on a two-drop, and the drain trigger converts the sacrifice theme into reach. A 60.2% GIH on an 85.9% play rate is a real card.
Stir Up Trouble: The card that makes black sacrifice work. One mana to destroy any creature is the best rate in the set, and the additional cost is nearly free when you have a spent equipment or an amass token to feed it. An 85.4% play rate on a common with a real cost says the fodder is always there.
Stony-Voiced Goblins: Good B/R common and better than the −0.5 IWD reads. Two mana for a body that strips a card is a fine rate, and the goblin type plus a sacrificeable body matters in the amass deck. LoL was right that the sacrifice and equipment synergies outweigh the format's flashback cards.
Supper for Spiders: Unplayable outside a very specific board state — a 12.7% play rate with no measured win rate. It only functions after a mass trade in the same turn, which you can't reliably arrange, and the Food bodies arrive too late. Provisional read.
Balin, Loremaster: Overrated by the LoL play report — a −3.6 IWD is one of the worst among rares. Five mana for a 4/4 whose payoff is discarding your hand to redraw is a card that wants a board you don't have yet, and the wheel is often a downgrade. The 68.5% play rate is rarity bias.
Bombur, Gentle Dreamer: Playable R/W filler with a real drawback. A three-mana 5/3 is above rate, but not untapping without an enduring story means it's a wall until storied comes online. The −0.6 IWD is the cost of that gap; it's fine once your artifacts and legends accumulate.
Bothersome Noisemaker: Kill on sight, and one of the best uncommons in the set. A two-mana 2/2 that amasses on every noncreature spell turns removal and tricks into a growing army, and an 89.7% play rate with a 62.7% GIH means it is both universally played and actually winning. LoL's #1 red uncommon.
Burn, Burn, Tree and Fern: A premium red uncommon and better than LR's C. Six damage kills essentially anything in the set given damage-based removal caps at five elsewhere, and the two red mana afterwards fuels a real turn. A 60.9% GIH on an 89.9% play rate is a card that is both universally played and winning.
Dáin Ironfoot: A top-tier R/W rare and the equipment deck's best payoff. The Axe arrives attached, so it's immediately a threat, and granting double strike to every equipped attacker turns a normal attack into lethal. The +7.1 IWD and 92.4% play rate say it is close to a first pick.
Desert Were-Worm: The worst rare in the set by the numbers — 46.8% GIH and a −6.9 IWD. A 0/5 that needs Mountains to have any power and asks you to attack with twelve total power is a build-around for a deck that doesn't exist. Do not play it.
Desolation of Smaug: A situational sweeper and the 48.8% play rate says fewer than half of red decks want it. Three damage to each non-Dragon creature is symmetrical in a format where you're usually the one with the board, so it's a control card in an aggro format. Sideboard it.
Dori, Bearer of Friends: Efficient R/W common and the cleanest storied enabler in the set — a legend that makes an artifact is two of the three types on one card. A 3/2 trample for three is on rate. Curve a two-drop into Dori and you have an enduring story on turn three.
Dwarven Mauler: The LoL disagreement resolves toward Mark, but only just. A one-mana 2/1 that makes every equip cost two less is genuinely good in the dwarf deck — it's how R/W moves weapons around profitably — but the −1.8 IWD says it's a vanilla 2/1 too often. Wants four or five equipment.
Gandalf, Goblins' Bane: Overdrafted on the mythic slot — ALSA 1.8 and 84.7% play against a 55.3% GIH and +1.2 IWD. Growing on noncreature spells wants a spell density B/R doesn't run, and a 2/3 body doesn't hold the ground. Playable, not the bomb its pick position implies.
Gandalf, Spark Starter: Strong top end for B/R, and the six-mana cost is the only thing holding it back. Three damage divided cleans up after a favourable attack or just kills two creatures outright, which is worth a lot when removal is this scarce. Take it highly; play exactly one.
Getaway Barrel: Unplayable, and the numbers are unambiguous — a 4.3% play rate with no measured win rate. Four mana that does nothing until it dies, then hits a random creature off thirteen cards, is not a plan in a format decided on the ground. Provisional only for lack of games.
Glóin the Mighty: A good B/R and R/W playable, and the adventure is the reason. Easy Pickings sweeping one damage off every opposing creature wrecks recruit tokens and small amass armies, then you cast a 4/3 that ramps. Two cards in one at a fair rate.
Goblin-town Flunkies: A fine B/R common but overrated by LLU's #1 ranking. The −2.5 IWD is honest: two bodies for two mana is good for sacrifice and equipment, but neither body is threatening on its own. Good glue, not a card that wins games.
Gundabad Opportunist: Reasonable red filler that serves up a two-for-one. A 4/2 for four trades with anything and the exiled card is real value, but the −1.3 IWD says the body dies too easily to be a threat. Fine in B/R, unremarkable.
Iron Hills Stalwart: A cut. Five mana for a 4/5 that reattaches an equipment is exactly the kind of top-end that arrives after the game is decided, and the −2.2 IWD with a 27.0% play rate confirms nobody wants it. LR's D was right.
Last Light of Durin's Day: Unplayable at 5.9% play with no measured win rate. Six Mountain triggers to tutor a Dragon is a Constructed build-around; you will not get there in a two-colour Limited deck. Provisional.
The Misty Mountains Cold: Better than its C− grade. Four Treasures across four turns ramps and fixes, and the payoff on sacrifice is real value. The +4.8 IWD at 79.8% play says it does more than it reads, though three mana that affects nothing immediately is the cost.
Misty Mountains Raider: Very good in B/R, with the caveat both LoL hosts flag: no haste means it must survive a turn before it does anything. When it lives, amassing 2 on every attack ends games quickly. An 85.4% play rate at five mana says the goblin decks are always happy to have it.
Óin the Brave: Marginal R/W filler. A 1/3 blocks the format's cheap attackers and storied is easy to switch on, but the rummage activation costs a card and the −0.2 IWD says it contributes nothing beyond the body. Playable in a dwarf deck short on two-drops.
Pinecone Strike: Red's premium common and among the best commons in the set. Two mana at instant speed to deal three *and exile* answers nearly every important uncommon, and the artifact-token mode is real upside against equipment and Treasures. A 91.2% play rate confirms LoL's read that it is broken.
Ragged Short Spear: A Tormenting Voice with an equipment stapled on, and that's the right way to evaluate it. The equip cost of three is unaffordable in a fast format, so you're paying two mana to loot up a card and leave a storied enabler behind. Fine filler in R/W.
Smaug, the Great Calamity: A legitimate sleeper at common and Ben's read holds up. Spew Flame for five mana is a removal spell that answers almost anything, then the 5/5 flier arrives later as a finisher — two cards in one slot. Slow, but the 62.9% play rate shows people found the value.
Smaug the Magnificent: A first-pick mythic and one of the format's premier threats. Four mana for a 4/3 flying haste already ends games quickly, and the Treasure engine means the attack trigger scales every turn while ramping you. A +9.5 IWD at ALSA 1.4 is close to the top of the set.
Smaug's Fury: A cut at 16.5% play. Generic pump with no payoffs behind it is the weakest card type in a format with this little instant-speed interaction, and the −2.4 IWD confirms it.
Snowslope Hunter: The free, no-mana sacrifice outlet is the reason to play it — it's the only repeatable one in the set, which makes it the engine for the attrition build of B/R. The −2.3 IWD reflects an understated 2/3 body; the ability is what you're buying.
Stone-Giant of High Pass: A genuine bomb and an early pick at ALSA 2.4. A 7/7 that leaves a 3/1 blocker behind every attack is nearly impossible to answer with damage-based removal, and the artifact-sacrifice ability converts its own tokens into reach. The 58.2% understates it because seven mana is a real cost.
Thorin, Mountain-king: A build-around mythic that pays off hard when built for. On entry it attaches every Equipment you control and then machine-guns something for that creature's power — with five or more equipment that is a one-sided blowout. The +6.8 IWD and ALSA 1.8 confirm it; without equipment it's a four-mana 3/4.
Tidings of War: A genuine sleeper that plays better than its −1.6 IWD. Turn-one amass 1 curves into a two-drop and attacks immediately; later, flashing it back for amass 3 dumps three counters onto an existing Army. Good to discard, good to mill, and it fuels the sacrifice deck.
Attercop: A genuinely good green common and better than its C− grade. Reach and deathtouch on a two-drop trades with anything, blanks the format's few fliers, and pairs perfectly with Quarrel. The +2.0 IWD says it does more than block.
Bejeweled Warg: Excellent and an early pick at ALSA 2.0. Two mana for a 3/2 trample is above rate on its own, and the combat trigger either grows your wolves or ramps you. A +6.4 IWD on an 86.3% play rate makes this one of green's best cards.
Beorn, Reluctant Host: Below replacement at 49.9% GIH with a −3.3 IWD. A five-mana 5/5 trample sounds fine until you notice the format kills you before it matters, and the extra-land adventure does nothing in a two-colour deck. A 39.9% play rate is honest.
Beorn the Fierce: A first-pick mythic and a genuine bomb — a +11.7 IWD at ALSA 1.5. Even with no other Bears it's a five-mana 6/6 trample that grants +2/+2 and trample to another creature every combat, so it represents roughly ten power for five mana. Drawing two once you have three Bears is upside, not the plan.
Beorn's Hospitality: Reasonable green uncommon with a real late-game mode. Landfall counters accumulate quietly and the seven-mana animation gives a flooded draw a land-sized threat. The +3.5 IWD is honest value; Ben's #1 green uncommon is a touch high.
Boughside Wanderers: Fine G/U top end and a two-for-one at common, but the curve position is the problem — black and blue get their two-for-ones at three mana rather than six. Playable in a ramp deck, never a reason to be green. The 53.3% is about right.
Cantankerous Keepers: A trap at rare. Affinity for Elves only discounts it in the format's worst archetype, and a 51.6% GIH on six mana says the discount rarely materialises. G/U doesn't have the elf density to make this castable on time.
Dancing from Dark to Dawn: A first-pick mythic and possibly the hardest card in the set to answer — there is almost no enchantment removal. Every creature spell dumps counters and every land makes a 2/2, so it takes over a stalled board unassisted. ALSA 1.6 confirms it is taken immediately.
Down in the Valley: Middling in a bad archetype. The Saga ramps then makes bears, which is fine value, but it does nothing the turn it lands and G/U is five points behind the field. A 55.4% GIH is respectable; the deck it lives in isn't.
Galion, Elvenking's Butler: Narrower than it reads and the −1.1 IWD shows it. Copying Galion's stats onto another attacker needs a second real creature and a profitable attack; without both it's a four-mana 4/4. Playable in G/U, which is the format's worst deck.
Gigantic Big Bear: Overdrafted on stats — ALSA 2.5 and 79.7% play against a 52.4% GIH. Hexproof and haste on a 10/7 that can't be countered reads unbeatable, but seven mana in a format that ends around turn eight means you often die holding it. Play it as your only top-end, not as a reason to be green.
Guardian of the Halls: Filler. A two-mana 2/2 trample is on rate and the seven-mana pump gives a flooded draw something to do, but 52.8% GIH says it does little else. A late green playable.
Little Bear: A cut at 30.9% play and a −3.2 IWD. Three mana for a 3/2 flash that untaps something is a trick without a payoff — there aren't enough Bears to make the counter clause matter. LR's D is correct.
Mirkwood Pathmaker: Overperforms its grades and both guide reads. A three-mana body that scales with lands is exactly the cheap four-power creature B/G needs, and the +5.0 IWD on an 87.5% play rate says it is doing real work. LR's C/C− is too low; trust the data here.
Nasty Little Rabbit: Very good in B/G and a genuine one-drop threat, though the guides oversold it slightly. It needs ferocious online to grow, which realistically means turn four, and Mark's concern about enabler timing is visible in the 58.9% rather than something higher. Still one of the better one-drops in the set.
The Notary Hobbits: A trap at rare. Three bodies for five mana sounds fine until you notice they're 1/1s in a format where removal can't kill small creatures but combat certainly can. A 31.0% play rate and no measured win rate say most players correctly leave it out. Provisional.
Old Fat Spider: Important for a structural reason more than a statistical one — at 6/7 it is one of only two creatures at common or uncommon that damage-based removal simply cannot kill. The 53.6% GIH reflects six mana in a fast format, but as a top-end blocker that ends ground stalls it does its job.
Ordinary Bear: A French-vanilla 4/5 and a genuinely fine playable — five toughness blocks essentially everything in a format where damage removal caps at five, and four power turns on ferocious. The 39.9% play rate is too low; this is a real B/G card.
Part in Friendship: Slow value in the wrong format. Five mana that does nothing until your creatures start dying is backwards here, and the −1.8 IWD reflects it. The 62.1% play rate is people trusting the rare slot.
Quarrel: Green's only real removal and the one common both LR and LLU agreed on. Instant-speed bite is reliable here because green's creatures are the biggest in the format, and it pairs perfectly with deathtouch on Attercop. An 83.4% play rate says every green deck runs it.
Radagast of Rhosgobel: The card LoL and LLU both failed to rank, and the data says they were right to skip it. A 50.9% GIH despite ALSA 2.3 and 81.0% play means people first-pick it and it underdelivers — a 2/5 that discounts one creature a turn doesn't affect the board enough in a format this fast.
Through the Forest Gate: Unplayable. Eight mana for lands and life in a format decided by turn eight is a non-card, and an 8.8% play rate with no measured win rate confirms nobody is finding a home for it. Provisional only for lack of games.
Troll Negotiations: Strong when it resolves, and the reason to be cautious is exactly what Ben said — four mana at sorcery speed into open mana is a real risk. Two counters plus a fight kills their best creature and leaves a four-power body for ferocious. The 55.2% reflects the times it gets blown out.
Warg Tactics: A worthwhile sideboard card and a reasonable maindeck one-of in B/G. The flying mode answers a real gap — B/G has essentially no reach — and the trample-plus-hexproof mode protects a bomb or forces lethal. The 53.9% is what a situational trick looks like.
Wargling: Playable B/G filler. Two mana for a 2/2 is on rate and granting the team trample on a ferocious attack occasionally converts a stalled board, but it needs the four-power creature first. The −0.9 IWD says it's a body more often than a payoff.
Wilderland Scrounger: The LR split resolves toward D+. A 51.8% GIH and −1.9 IWD say five mana for a 3/6 that only pays off on a ferocious attack is too slow. Its one virtue is the 6 toughness, which damage-based removal cannot touch.
Wood Elves: The LoL and LR split resolves toward Ben's dismissal. A 52.3% GIH says a three-mana 1/1 is a bad rate even with the untapped Forest attached, and it only makes sense in G/U — the format's worst archetype. Playable there, a cut elsewhere.
Woodland Weavemaster: A build-around that needs a deck that doesn't exist. Elf-restricted mana is only good with twelve or more elves, and G/U is the format's worst archetype by five points. The +3.5 IWD shows it works when assembled; the 60.8% play rate shows it usually isn't.
Bard, King of Dale: Underwhelming for a mythic at 53.6% GIH. Six mana for a 3/5 that doubles draws and tokens is a value engine arriving after the game is decided, and W/U wants to be curving out rather than durdling. The 74.4% play rate is rarity bias.
Bard the Bowman: The W/U signpost, and better than its D+ grade or its absence from both LLU lists suggested. A 1/3 reach blocks the format's cheap attackers, and the +5.3 IWD shows the counter-and-lifelink trigger swings combat more than it reads. Good in its deck, unplayable outside it.
Bard's Company: One of the best cards in the set and the strongest argument that W/U is real. A +10.8 IWD is enormous: flash makes it a combat trick, the anthem swings every attack, and it recruits twice. Take it over almost anything.
Bifur, Melodic Rider: LoL called it terrible and the data agrees more than LR's B does. Six mana for a 4/5 in a deck built to end games early is the wrong curve slot, and doubling dwarf triggers only matters if you already have a board. The −1.1 IWD is the honest read.
Bolg of the North: Good but not the best uncommon in the set, contra LoL. A −0.9 IWD on a five-mana 5/5 says the sacrifice trigger often isn't available or isn't profitable — you need a creature worth eating and a target worth hitting. Strong in a built B/R deck, mediocre elsewhere.
Bolg's Company: Mediocre for a rare. A two-mana 2/2 with conditional haste and a sacrifice-for-mana ability is a support card, not a threat, and the −0.7 IWD confirms it. Playable in a dedicated goblin deck; a late pick otherwise.
The Chief Warg: Overrated by every guide and the data is blunt — a −3.3 IWD on the B/G signpost. Four mana for a 3/3 that doesn't itself have four power means it can't turn on its own trigger, which is the design miss both LoL hosts flagged. Playable, not a payoff.
Chief Warg's Company: A premium B/G rare — 64.1% GIH and +8.1 IWD at ALSA 1.9. It makes a 2/2 Wolf every upkeep whether or not it can attack, so a 5/3 trample that's stuck at home is still building a board. The attack restriction is much less of a cost than it reads.
Dáin's Company: A premium R/W rare — a +9.2 IWD at 81.8% play. A two-mana 2/2 that digs four for a Dwarf or Equipment is a two-for-one on turn two, and conditional lifelink matters in the races R/W plays. The hit rate is high enough in a real dwarf deck.
Duskwatch Hunter: The most important common in B/G and the reason ferocious functions at all. It is the only cheap common that reliably makes a four-power creature — drop the counter on itself — and it can't be blocked by the format's many 1/1 tokens. The 56.9% undersells its enabling role.
Dwalin, Weaponmaster: Excellent in R/W and better than its C+ grade. First strike on a two-drop is already good in a format decided by ground combat, and hone counters accumulate every attack so the equipment deck's clock accelerates. The +6.2 IWD is real; take it early.
Eagle's Rescue: Solid W/U uncommon that rewards the archetype's exact plan. +2/+2 and flying turns a recruit token into a real clock, and the graveyard recursion means pitching it to a recruit trigger is upside rather than a loss. The four-mana rate is why it isn't higher.
Fearsome Goblin Pair: Solid B/R glue and the rare card you're happy to have die. Amass 4 on death means it trades up against anything and feeds sacrifice outlets for free. The −1.0 IWD is misleading; it's a body plus four counters, not a value engine.
Goblin Plate Mail: One of the best commons in the set and LoL's enthusiasm is justified — an 86.5% play rate at ALSA 4.5 means it's played nearly always and still wheels. Two mana for a 2/1 menace body that leaves an equipment behind is two cards, and menace makes a stacked Army nearly unblockable.
The Great Goblin: A strong B/R rare at ALSA 2.0 and 87.5% play. Every amass trigger becomes two damage to the face, which converts a grindy board into a real clock, and the death trigger refills your hand. Fragile — no ETB and no protection — which is what the −0.8 IWD is measuring.
Large Bear: A pure rate card and exactly what B/G wants. Five mana for a 5/5 with reach, trample and haste means it attacks immediately, blocks fliers, and pushes through the format's chump blockers. An 89.1% play rate at ALSA 3.0 says it wheels less than it should.
Mirkwood Nurturer: The LoL and LLU disagreement resolves to the middle — a 54.2% GIH is a fine playable, not a top common. Bouncing an ETB creature is real value but costs you tempo, and G/U rarely has the board to spare. One copy is fine; Mark's top-three ranking is too high.
Nori, Teller of Tales: Marginal, and the −2.5 IWD is the tell. A two-mana 2/2 legend is fine storied fodder for R/W and the first-strike trigger occasionally steals a combat, but it does nothing on its own. LoL split on it; the data sides with Ben's C−.
Patient Instructor: A clean W/U common and the archetype's most reliable enabler. Vigilance plus a 1/1 token is real board presence, and the +4.7 IWD says the recruit trigger is doing more than card selection. Despite the hybrid cost, it only belongs in a recruit deck.
Silvan Reveler: The primer's biggest disagreement, and the data sides with Alex. A 52.3% GIH is poor for a card LoL called insanely strong — the effect is real but it lives in Simic, the worst archetype by five points, and four mana that doesn't affect the board is a losing rate here. Good card, wrong format.
Smaug, Wicked Worm: A strong B/R rare and an early pick at ALSA 2.0. A five-mana 5/5 flier is already above the format's answer rate given damage removal caps at five, and the Treasure clauses turn it into a value engine against artifact decks. The 56.0% understates a card that just wins unanswered.
Thorin Oakenshield: The R/W signpost and a fine two-drop, though the −1.6 IWD is a caution. A 3/2 trample for two is good rate, and ward 1 on your board is genuinely annoying — but you lose the ward the moment Thorin dies, and he's a combat creature you'll be trading off early.
Thranduil, Sindarin Liege: The best card in G/U and the +6.9 IWD proves it does the work. An elf lord that makes a token on every land drop builds a board by itself, and the Mulch adventure means it's never dead early. The archetype is bad; this card isn't.
Thranduil, the Elvenking: Effectively unplayable at 33.0% play with no measured win rate — three colours in a format where splashing is a trap. The activated-abilities clause needs an elf graveyard you won't have. Provisional read on a card few are casting.
Thranduil's Company: The best card in G/U by a distance and a +11.6 IWD proves it. Two counters and vigilance on every land drop, plus an extra land drop with any other Elf, snowballs fast. Splashable as a plain five-drop even without elves — and note they can't respond to a land drop, so the first trigger is guaranteed.
Tom, Bert, and William: A first-pick rare and a nightmare to fight through. Instant-speed, not once per turn, so leaving one mana up with a four-power creature around threatens a huge draw; and it returns as an artifact when it dies, so removal doesn't fully answer it. The +6.0 IWD is earned.
The Arkenstone: Effectively an auto-include — a 98.9% play rate and ALSA 1.1 mean it is first-picked and played every single time. A permanent anthem that draws a card every turn wins any game that goes long, and the adventure tutors a legend when you need a body first. CGB's A is correct.
The Black Arrow: A trap despite LR's B−. A −5.0 IWD is one of the worst in the set: one damage rarely kills anything given removal can't handle small creatures anyway, the Dragon clause is nearly blank, and three mana for a +1/+1 equipment is unplayable rate.
Dwarven Mattock: A build-around: LR's split of B in dwarves and D outside is exactly right. Auto-attaching for +2/+2 and ward 1 on a two-mana artifact is excellent when you have ten dwarves, and unplayable when you have three. Check your count before taking it.
Giant's Boulder: Close to unplayable at 49.0% GIH and 21.2% play. The scry 2 is the only real text; the mana filtering matters little in a two-colour format and seven mana to destroy a permanent never happens. Counts for storied, which is its one job.
Glamdring, Foe-hammer: Unplayable at 11.3% play with no measured win rate. Discounting instants and sorceries by an equipped creature's power is a Constructed ability in a creature-combat format, and the mill adventure fills a graveyard nobody here uses. Provisional.
Key to the Side-Door: A cut, and LR's F is right. Both abilities cost mana you'd rather spend on the board, and the draw-two clause requires a duplicate legend in hand. A 12.1% play rate with no win rate is the verdict.
My Precious: A trap despite ALSA 1.9 and 85.0% play. A 51.0% GIH with a flat IWD says making one creature unblockable and hexproof doesn't win games in a format decided by board size, and equipping costs mana plus life. The Allure of Power adventure is the better half.
Orcrist, Goblin-cleaver: The clearest trap in the set. ALSA 1.5 and an 85.8% play rate mean people first-pick and play it every time, and it still posts a 51.6% GIH — a mythic equipment costing three plus three to move is far too slow for this format. Take a good creature instead.
Sting, Bilbo's Sword: A trap despite the rare slot and the 77.8% play rate. A −3.7 IWD and a sub-50% GIH are damning: the hone counters scale off *their* board, so it is weakest exactly when you are behind, and three to re-equip is unaffordable in a fast format.
Thrór's Map: Fine but overrated by LR's B+. Fetching a basic to hand and a repeatable loot is real in a grindy deck, but two mana that doesn't affect the board is a poor turn in this format, and the 54.1% GIH reflects that. Playable, not a high pick.
Well-Worn Spatula: Close to unplayable and the 21.6% play rate confirms it. One mana for a +1/+1 equipment and 2 life is the definition of a 23rd card, though it does count for storied and gives Thorin, Mountain-king another attachment. Play it only to reach equipment critical mass.
Elven Passage: A reasonable land that mostly just fixes. Sacrificing for a basic costs you tempo, and the behold-an-Elf untap clause only matters in G/U. A 79.3% play rate with a modest +1.2 IWD is the profile of a land people include without it changing games.
Elvenking's Halls: A weak land in the weakest archetype. Entering tapped costs real tempo, the sacrifice mode needs an Elf worth pumping, and the 51.9% GIH is the lowest of the cycle. Play one only if you're committed to G/U.
Goblin-town: A reasonable B/R land in the best archetype, with the usual tapland caveat. The −2.6 IWD is mostly the tempo cost of entering tapped; the sacrifice mode gives a flooded goblin deck a way to push counters onto its Army. Play one.
Hobbit Hole: A near-free inclusion at 86.4% play. Sacrificing for a basic is fine fixing, and halflingcycling means a flooded draw converts a land into a real card. The −0.5 IWD is the tempo of a land that doesn't tap for mana; play it anyway.
Iron Hills: A fine inclusion in R/W and nothing more. Entering tapped is a real cost in a fast format, but the sacrifice ability gives a dwarf deck a late-game mana sink. The −2.6 IWD is mostly the tapland tax; play one or two, not three.
Lake-town: Fine in W/U and nothing more. Entering tapped costs real tempo here, but the late-game sink of two counters on a Human gives a flooded draw something to do. Play one; the +2.0 IWD is mostly the deck it appears in rather than the land itself.
The Lonely Mountain: An excellent R/W land and effectively free once you have any Equipment. It usually enters untapped in the deck that wants it, and the Dwarf-making ability gets genuinely cheap with a few equipment out, giving flooded draws a real mana sink. A 90.3% play rate says the dwarf decks always run it.
Mirkwood: A reasonable B/G land whose tapped-land cost is real in this format. The sacrifice mode gives a flooded draw a way to push through, and hitting Bears, Spiders or Wolves covers most of the archetype. One copy, not three.
